bug_semantics: On Ruby 3.1.x, acronym-aware name conversion with `/([A-Z]+)([A-Z][a-z])/` performs polynomial (quadratic) backtracking on a long run of capital letters. Tool/agent/class names can reach this conversion, so an attacker-controlled very long name can consume excessive CPU and cause denial of service.
flaw_origin: The flaw originated in `cd0ca3e859d784cf0441f1872de706579d546db3`, which first replaced explicitly supplied tool names with automatic class-name derivation and added the vulnerable two-`gsub` CamelCase-to-snake_case implementation in `lib/ruby_llm/tool.rb` lines 27-32. Later normalization/refactor/revert commits preserved those regexes, and `17a0ec4f01c2ac1186599551b9ba0c13fad54334` moved the same logic into `RubyLLM::Utils.underscore` and shared it with agent/tool-choice naming; that move is not the BIC.
ai_marker: absent — the BIC commit object identifies both author and committer as Carmine Paolino (@crmne), has `committerAttribution:false`, an empty body (`bodyMessageHtml:""`), no Co-Authored-By or Generated-with trailer, and no bot identity.
evidence: Advisory mechanism and vulnerable snapshot: NVD and the reporter gist identify Ruby 3.1.x, `RubyLLM::Utils.underscore`, polynomial ReDoS, and vulnerable snapshot `fa6f279847d6d7027814539d9c0dfc3bbdfd2a83`: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-67991 and https://gist.github.com/Zykis1024/9f2d68fa3fd4e3a0ab83063bbe61a8e2; cited vulnerable line: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/blob/fa6f279847d6d7027814539d9c0dfc3bbdfd2a83/lib/ruby_llm/utils.rb#L13.

Smallest BIC: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/cd0ca3e859d784cf0441f1872de706579d546db3 adds in `lib/ruby_llm/tool.rb` the exact vulnerable chain `.gsub(/([A-Z]+)([A-Z][a-z])/, '\1_\2').gsub(/([a-z\d])([A-Z])/, '\1_\2')` while changing tools from caller-supplied names to class-derived names; the same commit declares source version `0.1.0.pre10`.

Direct-parent absence: the BIC object names sole parent `2b7ff0eefcca66ec65727bfb4b49fa6dd0d20e99`; its tree at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/crmne/ruby_llm/2b7ff0eefcca66ec65727bfb4b49fa6dd0d20e99/lib/ruby_llm/tool.rb has neither regex and instead stores the explicit `name` passed to `Tool.define`. Parent commit: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/2b7ff0eefcca66ec65727bfb4b49fa6dd0d20e99.

Lifecycle/history: `d34592efe00697457ac020cd5ec80a13c2827fed` only prepended character normalization while preserving the regexes (https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/d34592efe00697457ac020cd5ec80a13c2827fed); `1ba6a78de96af352ba8408c9dd7ac50dc138c36c` moved them into a helper and `818b8ca2d38c271fb5b96b2404dc4c83313c132c` restored them inline (https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/1ba6a78de96af352ba8408c9dd7ac50dc138c36c and https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/818b8ca2d38c271fb5b96b2404dc4c83313c132c). `17a0ec4f01c2ac1186599551b9ba0c13fad54334` extracted the same vulnerable code to `lib/ruby_llm/utils.rb` and routed tool/agent naming through it: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/17a0ec4f01c2ac1186599551b9ba0c13fad54334.

Version boundary: the BIC changes `lib/ruby_llm/version.rb` from `0.1.0.pre9` to `0.1.0.pre10`, establishing the source lower boundary. The earliest retained local tag, `0.1.0.pre42` at `a96915d238ed58aa3083051b0667466cacd7974b`, still contains both vulnerable regexes: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/blob/0.1.0.pre42/lib/ruby_llm/tool.rb. The latest release/tag is `1.16.0` at `2cf34b9264a5d6cd4ea7868c6989232b2bedf2c1` (released 2026-06-09) and also retains the vulnerable pair: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/blob/1.16.0/lib/ruby_llm/tool.rb and https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/releases/tag/1.16.0. Thus retained prerelease `0.1.0.pre42` and stable releases `1.0.0` through `1.16.0` are on the vulnerable side; the advisory itself supplies no package range and says the released range was not yet determined.

Direct fix: https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/9d75b033d7d00c4e1baa9b0afb4828faa8bd6602 explicitly cites CVE-2026-67991, explains the quadratic backtracking, replaces the capture/backreference regex chain in `lib/ruby_llm/utils.rb` with fixed-width lookaround boundary matching, and adds a 100,000-capital regression case. Its parent source remains vulnerable: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/crmne/ruby_llm/dd3c84812598/lib/ruby_llm/utils.rb; main is fixed: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/crmne/ruby_llm/main/lib/ruby_llm/utils.rb.

Fix/release boundary: fix `9d75b033d7d00c4e1baa9b0afb4828faa8bd6602` landed 2026-08-17, after latest release `1.16.0` (2026-06-09). No fixed gem release/tag is present as of the audit date; the fix is on main.

BIC-only AI attribution: the embedded BIC commit-object metadata at https://github.com/crmne/ruby_llm/commit/cd0ca3e859d784cf0441f1872de706579d546db3 records author and committer Carmine Paolino (@crmne), `committerAttribution:false`, empty body, and no trailers. No later commit's metadata was used for attribution.
reasoning: The vulnerable behavior must be traced before considering AI attribution. The advisory points to `Utils.underscore` at a 2026 snapshot, but history shows that `17a0ec4f01c2ac1186599551b9ba0c13fad54334` merely extracted already-existing name-conversion lines. The earliest commit that actually wrote the vulnerable regexes and made class-derived tool names reach them is `cd0ca3e859d784cf0441f1872de706579d546db3`; its immediate parent has neither regex and accepts an explicit name, proving parent-tree absence. Subsequent normalization, helper extraction, revert, and Utils extraction preserved the mechanism and expanded/centralized its callers. The BIC's `0.1.0.pre10` version bump precedes retained affected tags; endpoint source checks show the flaw in `0.1.0.pre42` and latest release `1.16.0`. Commit `9d75b033d7d00c4e1baa9b0afb4828faa8bd6602` is the direct fix because it removes the backtracking expression from the shared function and replaces it with fixed-width lookarounds; it is on main but postdates the latest release, so there is not yet a fixed release boundary. Finally, only the BIC commit object was inspected for AI attribution: its human author/committer identity, empty body, and absence of AI/bot trailers provide no BIC-level AI evidence, so the causal verdict is NOT_AI.
